abstract: Dysregulation of long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) and interferon signaling contributes to tumorigenesis and progression; however, their crosstalk in tumor biology remains poorly understood. Here, we showed that TSPEAR-AS2, an lncRNA mediated by METTL1, activates the interferon signaling pathway in esophageal cancer (ESCA). Clinically, we conducted a pan-cancer investigation and identified TSPEAR-AS2 as a novel ESCA-related lncRNA that predicts a worse patient prognosis. The high expression of TSPEAR-AS2 was validated in multiple ESCA cohorts, demonstrating that this lncRNA had good diagnostic performance. METTL1, an RNA N7-methylguanosine (m7G) methyltransferase, was positively correlated with TSPEAR-AS2 expression in ESCA tissues, and METTL1 was found to induce TSPEAR-AS2 expression in ESCA cells. Functionally, the up-regulation of TSPEAR-AS2 promoted proliferation, cell cycle progression, migration, and stemness in ESCA cells, whereas its knockdown attenuated these malignant phenotypes. Furthermore, both TSPEAR-AS2 deficiency and antisense oligonucleotide (ASO)-based intratumoral intervention could significantly suppress tumor growth in vivo. Mechanistically, quantitative proteomic analysis revealed that TSPEAR-AS2 ablation altered the expression of functional proteins related to interferon signaling pathways, such as HLA-E, IRF3, and IFITs. These findings identify a previously unrecognized role of the METTL1/TSPEAR-AS2/interferon signaling axis in ESCA development and suggest that TSPEAR-AS2 is a potential prognostic indicator and therapeutic vulnerability for this malignancy.

Materials and methods
Data mining
GEPIA (
http://gepia2.cancer-pku.cn/#index
) is an integrated online tumor analysis server that includes expression data and prognostic information for more than 30 cancers. Our study used this database for gene expression and prognostic analysis. ENCORI (
https://rnasysu.com/encori/index.php
), an open tumor database that integrates molecular expression data and patient survival information for 17 cancers, was used this tool for gene expression and correlation analysis. TSPEAR-AS2 expression data in three ESCA cohorts, including TCGA,
GSE53622
, and
GSE53624
, were obtained from The Cancer Genome Atlas (
https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov/
) and GEO database (
https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gds/?term
=). The Kaplan–Meier Plotter
17
was employed to investigate the prognostic value of TSPEAR-AS2 in ESCA. The LncACTdb 3.0
18
was utilized to predict potential functions of TSPEAR-AS2. The UALCAN database (
https://ualcan.path.uab.edu/
) was used for analyzing the expression of TSPEAR-AS2 in cancer subtypes.
Receiver operating character (ROC) curve and enrichment analysis
The ROC curve analysis was used to evaluate the diagnostic potential of TSPEAR-AS2 in multiple ESCA cohorts. The larger the area under the curve (AUC), the better the diagnostic performance. Co-expressed genes of TSPEAR-AS2 in ESCA was obtained from GEPIA database. The Reactome enrichment analysis was performed using the online server WebGestalt (
https://www.webgestalt.org/
).
Cell culture and transfection
Human ESCA cell lines (TE1, EC1, KYSE70, and KYSE450) and an esophageal epithelial cell line (Het-1A) were grown in RPMI 1640 medium containing 10% fetal bovine serum and 1% penicillin–streptomycin solution. Adherent cells were digested by trypsin and then kept in a 37 ℃ incubator containing 5% carbon dioxide. INTERFERin, Lipo3000, and HiTransG A reagents were used to transfect siRNA (si-AS2#1, si-AS2#2), recombinant plasmids (OE-METTL1, OE-AS2), and recombinant lentivirus (sh-AS2), respectively. The siRNA sequence is shown in Supplementary Table
1
.
Quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR)
Adherent ESCA cells were digested with trypsin and collected in a centrifuge tube. Total RNA was extracted from the cells using the Trizol reagent, and the concentration and purity of the extracted RNA were subsequently measured. After the RNA was reverse transcribed, qRT-PCR was performed using SYBR GREEN reagent (Novoprotein, China) on the reaction system (AB, USA). Subsequently, the relative expression of interest genes was analyzed, with the GAPDH gene serving as the internal reference. The sequence of primers was shown in Supplementary Table
1
.
Western blot
Adherent ESCA cells were digested with trypsin and then collected in centrifuge tubes. The total proteins were extracted from ESCA cells using RIPA buffer. Loading buffer was added to the proteins and incubated at 100 ℃ for 10 min for denaturation. Subsequently, the proteins were subjected to polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis, membrane transfer, blocking, primary antibodies incubation (anti-GAPDH, Bioworld; anti-METTL1, Sino Biological), and secondary antibody incubation. Finally, ECL luminescent reagent was added to PVDF membrane, and multifunctional luminescence analyzer was used for detection.
Cell counting kit 8 (CCK-8) assay
The effect of TSPEAR-AS2 knockdown or over-expression on the proliferation of ESCA cells was determined by CCK-8 (Cellor Lab, China) assay. In short, transfected cells were uniformly inoculated in 96-well plates, and cells in each well were incubated with 10 µL of CCK-8 solution for about 3 h at 37 °C. Absorbance at 450 nm was measured at pre-determined time points using a microplate reader.
Flow cytometry
A propidium iodide (PI) kit (7sea Biotech, China) and flow cytometry were used to detect the effects of TSPEAR-AS2 knockdown or over-expression on the ESCA cell cycle. Briefly, adherent cells were digested with trypsin and collected in a centrifuge tube. The cells were fixed with pre-cooled 70% ethanol and incubated with PI solution for 30 min at 37 °C. Finally, the cell cycle was analyzed using a flow cytometer.
Transwell assay
Transwell assay was utilized to examine the effects of knockdown or over-expression of TSPEAR-AS2 on the metastatic ability of ESCA cells. Adherent transfected cells were digested with trypsin and collected in a centrifuge tube. The cells were suspended in fresh medium without fetal bovine serum (FBS). These cells were uniformly inoculated in the upper Transwell chamber, whereas a fresh medium containing 20% FBS was added to the lower chamber. After 48 h, the migrated cells were fixed, stained, and analyzed.
Tumor sphere formation assay
Tumor sphere formation assay was employed to evaluate the effects of knockdown or over-expression of TSPEAR-AS2 on the stemness of ESCA cells. Briefly, transfected ESCA cells were digested with trypsin and collected in a centrifuge tube. The cells were suspended with tumor sphere-forming medium (DMEM/F12 medium containing 0.4% BSA, 20 ng/mL EGF, 10 ng/mL bFGF, 5 μg/mL insulin, and B27). 4 ml sphere-forming medium were added to the low-adhesion six-well plate and incubated at 37 °C for several days. The formation of tumor cells into spheres was observed and photographed using a microscope.
Tumor formation experiment
Tumor formation assay was used to investigate the effects of TSPEAR-AS2 knockdown on ESCA cell growth in vivo. Transfected KYSE70 cells (sh-NC or sh-AS2) were digested with trypsin and collected in a centrifuge tube. ESCA cells were suspended in normal saline and then subcutaneously inoculated into male nude BALB/c mice (Beijing Vital River Company, China). After tumor formation, the tumor volume was measured using the formula: length × width
2
× 0.5. Finally, the mice were euthanized via cervical dislocation and the tumors were finally isolated and photographed.
Tumor intervention experiment
Tumor intervention experiment was performed to observe the effect of TSPEAR-AS2 targeted by ASO on ESCA growth in vivo. Briefly, untransfected KYSE70 cells were subcutaneously inoculated into male nude BALB/c mice (Beijing HFK Bioscience Company, China). When the tumor size reached about 50 mm
3
, ASO-NC or ASO-AS2 (GenePharma) was injected into the tumor twice a week for three weeks. Subsequently, the mice were euthanized via cervical dislocation and the tumors were isolated and photographed.
Proteomics analysis
Quantitative proteomics analysis (PTMBIO, China) were employed to explore the potential mechanism through which TSPEAR-AS2 promoted ESCA progression. Briefly, ESCA cells were collected in a centrifuge tube and lysed with a buffer containing 1% SDS and 1% protease inhibitors to extract total proteins. After the concentration of the extracted proteins was determined, the proteins were digested and the obtained peptides were desalted using a Strata-X solid-phase extraction column. Subsequently, the peptides were dissolved in solvent A and directly loaded onto the reversed-phase analytical column for mass spectrometry.
Statistical analysis
All experimental results were expressed as the mean ± standard deviation. A t-test was used to compare data between groups. Data plotting and statistical analysis were performed using Graphpad Prism 9.0 and SPSS 19.0. A p-value less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. We confirm that all methods were performed in accordance with the relevant guidelines and regulations.

Tumor formation assay was used to investigate the effects of TSPEAR-AS2 knockdown on ESCA cell growth in vivo. Transfected KYSE70 cells (sh-NC or sh-AS2) were digested with trypsin and collected in a centrifuge tube. ESCA cells were suspended in normal saline and then subcutaneously inoculated into male nude BALB/c mice (Beijing Vital River Company, China). After tumor formation, the tumor volume was measured using the formula: length × width

body:
Introduction
Esophageal cancer (ESCA) is one of the most common malignancies and the seventh leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide. According to the Global Cancer Statistics, more than 440,000 people die of ESCA each year
1
. The incidence rates of the two most common histological subtypes of ESCA, namely squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) and adenocarcinoma (AC), show significant geographical differences, with SCC being the main subtype of ESCA in China
2
,
3
. Although patients with early-stage ESCA can benefit from surgery, most patients are unfortunately diagnosed at an advanced stage, missing the opportunity for surgical intervention. Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) represent an alternative treatment option for cancer; however, their adverse effects and their impact on prognosis are poorly understood. Studies have shown that ICIs may be associated with reversible hearing loss and hypertransaminasemia but may be beneficial in reducing the risk of neuropathy
4
–
6
. The albumin level is a potential prognostic indicator in patients with advanced cancer treated with ICIs
7
. Moreover, the Royal Marsden Hospital (RMH) Score and DNA damage response may be associated with the prognosis and treatment of cancer
8
,
9
. However, owing to the lack of effective treatment strategies, the five-year survival rate of patients with ESCA remains extremely low. Therefore, exploring key factors involved in the malignant progression of ESCA is of great significance for improving or optimizing its clinical treatment.
The rapid development of high-throughput sequencing technology has improved the understanding of the dynamic changes in molecular processes involved in tumor development
10
. Thousands of differentially expressed molecules between normal samples and tumor samples have been identified by sequencing. These molecules include messenger RNAs (mRNAs) that have protein-coding ability and non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) that lack such capabilities. ncRNAs containing transcripts of more than 200 nucleotides in length are defined as long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs). Recent in-depth research has identified many dysregulated ESCA-related lncRNAs, such as TTN-AS1
11
, AGPG
12
, and ESCCAL-1
13
. However, lncRNA-mediated complex regulatory networks in ESCA remain largely unclear.
TSPEAR antisense RNA 2 (TSPEAR-AS2), located in the q22.3 region of chromosome 21, is a recently identified human disease-associated lncRNA. Studies investigating the role of TSPEAR-AS2 in human diseases, including cancer, are limited. TSPEAR-AS2 was initially reported to be involved in hypoxia-induced pulmonary hypertension through high-throughput sequencing
14
. Subsequently, the oncogenic role of TSPEAR-AS2 in gastric cancer and oral SCC was investigated
15
,
16
. Given that TSPEAR-AS2 is involved in cancer progression, investigating its expression profile, biological functions, and clinical relevance in human cancers is necessary.
In this study, we integrated clinical data from various tumor databases to map the expression landscape of TSPEAR-AS2 in human pan-cancer. TSPEAR-AS2 was found to be dysregulated in a variety of cancers, including ESCA. Notably, its higher expression was associated with shorter overall survival in patients with ESCA. Functionally, TSPEAR-AS2 knockdown inhibited proliferation, cell cycle progression, migration, and stemness in ESCA cells in vitro, and suppressed tumor growth in vivo. In addition, intratumoral injection of an ASO targeting TSPEAR-AS2 effectively inhibited the growth of ESCA tumors in vivo. Mechanistically, METTL1, an RNA m7G methyltransferase, was found to be responsible for the over-expression of TSPEAR-AS2 in ESCA. Quantitative proteomic analysis showed that down-regulation of TSPEAR-AS2 induced the suppression of interferon signaling in ESCA. Altogether, these findings suggest that TSPEAR-AS2 is a novel factor contributing to the development of ESCA and provide a rationale for targeting TSPEAR-AS2 to treat ESCA.

Results
Pan-cancer expression heterogeneity of TSPEAR-AS2
TSPEAR-AS2 is a recently identified disease-associated lncRNA. However, its role in human cancers is yet to be fully elucidated. To address this knowledge gap, we used clinical data from two tumor databases, GEPIA and ENCORI, to map the pan-cancer expression profile of TSPEAR-AS2. According to the GEPIA database, the expression of TSPEAR-AS2 was dysregulated in multiple cancers. For instance, its expression was decreased in cervical squamous cell carcinoma and endocervical adenocarcinoma (CESC), acute myeloid leukemia (LAML), lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), rectum adenocarcinoma (READ), testicular germ cell tumors (TGCT), thyroid carcinoma (THCA), and uterine corpus endometrial carcinoma (UCEC) (Fig.
1
a, b), whereas it was increased in ESCA and stomach adenocarcinoma (STAD) (Fig.
1
c). The expression of TSPEAR-AS2 was not significantly altered in other cancer types. Data from the ENCORI database showed that TSPEAR-AS2 expression was deregulated in seven cancer types. Its expression was down-regulated in THCA (Fig.
1
d) and up-regulated in colon adenocarcinoma (COAD), ESCA, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSC), kidney renal clear cell carcinoma (KIRC), liver hepatocellular carcinoma (LIHC), and STAD (Fig.
1
e). However, the expression of TSPEAR-AS2 was not significantly altered in other cancer types. These results suggest that TSPEAR-AS2 exhibits heterogeneous expression across cancers.

TSPEAR-AS2 was found to be dysregulated in nine cancer types, including CESC (306T vs 13N), LAML (173T vs 70N), LUAD (483T vs 347N), READ (92T vs 318N), TGCT (137T vs 165N), THCA (512T vs 337N), UCEC (174T vs 91N), ESCA (182T vs 286N), and STAD (408T vs 211N). (d-e) The ENCORI database was employed to characterize the expression profile of TSPEAR-AS2 in human pan-cancer. TSPEAR-AS2 was dysregulated in seven cancer types, including THCA (510T vs 58N), COAD (471T vs 41N), ESCA (162T vs 11N), HNSC (502T vs 44N), KIRC (535T vs 72N), LIHC (374T vs 50N), and STAD (375T vs 32N). TSPEAR-AS2 is up-regulated in ESCA and serves as a potential clinical biomarker
Data from GEPIA and ENCORI showed that TSPEAR-AS2 expression was dysregulated in ESCA, STAD, and THCA (Fig.
2
a). Therefore, we used the UALCAN database to analyze the expression of TSPEAR-AS2 in the subtypes of these three cancers. The results revealed significant differences in the expression of TSPEAR-AS2 among the subtypes. In ESCA, TSPEAR-AS2 expression was higher level in adenocarcinoma than in squamous cell carcinoma (Supplementary Fig.
1
a). In STAD, TSPEAR-AS2 expression was higher in AdenoNOS, IntAdenoNOS, and IntAdenoPapillary subtypes but lower in AdenoDiffuse and IntAdenoMucinouse subtypes (Supplementary Fig.
1
b). In THCA, TSPEAR-AS2 expression was higher in Classical and Follicular subtypes but lower in Tall subtypes (Supplementary Fig.
1
c). The heterogeneity of TSPEAR-AS2 expression among these subtypes highlights its potential as a precise therapeutic target.

The GEPIA database was used to analyze the relationship between TSPEAR-AS2 expression and patient survival in the three cancers. It was found that TSPEAR-AS2 was associated with the prognosis of ESCA but not with that of STAD or THCA (Fig.
2
b–d), implying that TSPEAR-AS2 might play a crucial role in ESCA progression. The over-expression of TSPEAR-AS2 in ESCA was validated in three independent ESCA cohorts (TCGA, 11N vs. 161T;
GSE53622
, 60N vs. 60T; and
GSE53624
, 119N vs. 119T) (Fig.
2
e). Subsequently, ROC analysis was used to evaluate the diagnostic value of TSPEAR-AS2 in ESCA. The results showed that TSPEAR-AS2 exhibited high diagnostic value in all three ESCA cohorts (Fig.
2
f–h). Using the Kaplan–Meier Plotter database, we found that high expression of TSPEAR-AS2 was a risk factor for both disease-free survival (Fig.
2
i) and overall survival (Fig.
2
j) in patients with ESCA. We further confirmed that TSPEAR-AS2 was up-regulated in ESCA cell lines by qRT-PCR (Fig.
2
k). These data collectively indicate that TSPEAR-AS2 is a promising diagnostic and prognostic biomarker for ESCA.
RNA m7G transferase METTL1 mediates the expression of TSPEAR-AS2
Post-transcriptional modifications, such as N6-nathyladenosine (m6A), 5-methylcytosine (m5C), and N7-methylguanosine (m7G), play a crucial role in regulating gene expression in eukaryotic cells. To explore the potential mechanism underlying the up-regulation of TSPEAR-AS2 in ESCA, we analyzed the reported epigenetic modification enzymes FTO (m6A)
19
, METTL3 (m6A)
20
, NSUN2 (m5C)
21
, NSUN6 (m5C)
22
, METTL1 (m7G)
23
, and WDR4 (m7G)
24
in relation to TSPEAR-AS2 using the GEPIA and ENCORI databases. The results showed that the expression of METTL1 or NSUN6 was positively correlated with TSPEAR-AS2 in ESCA tumors, respectively (Fig.
3
a, b). We then explored the expressions of METTL1 and NSUN6 in ESCA using GEPIA and ENCORI databases, and found that METTL1 (Fig.
3
c), but not NSUN6 (Fig.
3
d), was increased in ESCA tumors, suggesting that METTL1 was a key factor involved in the regulation of TSPEAR-AS2. Over-expression of METTL1 in ESCA cells (Supplementary Fig.
2
a) led to significant up-regulation of TSPEAR-AS2 (Fig.
3
e), suggesting that METTL1 induces the expression of TSPEAR-AS2.

Loss of TSPEAR-AS2 suppresses ESCA cell proliferation and cell cycle progression
We then performed bioinformatics analysis to investigate the potential biological function of TSPEAR-AS2 in ESCA. We conducted a Reactome enrichment analysis based on co-expressed genes of TSPEAR-AS2 and found that TSPEAR-AS2 was involved in ESCA cell proliferation and stemness regulation (Supplementary Fig.
2
b). In addition, LncACTdb 3.0 showed that TSPEAR-AS2 participated in cell growth and metastasis (Supplementary Fig.
2
c). Subsequently, both gain-of-function and loss-of-function assays were performed to assess the biological role of TSPEAR-AS2 in ESCA. Transfection with OE-AS2 (a recombinant lentivirus used to over-express TSPEAR-AS2) up-regulated TSPEAR-AS2 expression in ESCA cells (Fig.
4
a), whereas transfection with two siRNAs targeting TSPEAR-AS2 (si-AS2#1 and si-AS2#2) significantly decreased its expression in ESCA cells (Fig.
4
b). Results from CCK-8 experiments showed that over-expression of TSPEAR-AS2 accelerated the proliferation of ESCA cells (Fig.
4
c), whereas its knockdown inhibited the growth of ESCA cells (Fig.
4
d, e). Similarly, over-expression of TSPEAR-AS2 promoted ESCA cell cycle progression (Fig.
4
f), whereas its down-regulation arrested ESCA cell cycle at the G0/G1 phase (Fig.
4
g).

TSPEAR-AS2 promotes cell metastasis, stemness, and tumor growth in ESCA
Transwell and tumor sphere formation assays were employed to observe the effects of TSPEAR-AS2 on ESCA cell migration and stemness, respectively. The results illustrated that knockdown of TSPEAR-AS2 inhibited the metastatic ability of ESCA cells, whereas its enforced expression promoted ESCA cell migration (Fig.
5
a, b). Moreover, ablation of TSPEAR-AS2 suppressed the stem-like properties of ESCA cells, whereas its up-regulation enhanced cell stemness (Fig.

TSPEAR-AS2 is a potential therapeutic target for ESCA
Targeting key molecules via ASOs is considered a promising therapeutic strategy for cancer treatment. We synthesized an ASO targeting TSPEAR-AS2 and examined its effects on TSPEAR-AS2 in KYSE70 cells (Supplementary Fig.
2

To preliminarily evaluate the effectiveness of targeting TSPEAR-AS2 for the treatment of ESCA, we established a subcutaneous tumor-bearing model using nude mice, and injected ASO-AS2 into the tumors twice a week for three weeks. The results showed that ASO-AS2 significantly inhibited tumor growth in vivo (Fig.

Discussion
The onset and development of ESCA are extremely complex processes. A better understanding of the pathological mechanisms underlying ESCA can improve the diagnosis and treatment of patients. Emerging studies have revealed that the abnormal activation of interferon signaling and over-expression of lncRNAs can lead to tumor development and progression
25
,
26
. However, their crosstalk in ESCA remains poorly understood. In this study, we report that the disease-associated lncRNA TSPEAR-AS2 promotes the malignant phenotype of ESCA and regulates the interferon signaling pathway.
Over the past decade, hundreds of disease-associated lncRNAs have been identified using high-throughput sequencing. LncRNAs are considered promising disease markers and therapeutic targets owing to their specificity and stability
27
–
29
. Systematic biology helped identify the functions and mechanisms of some dysregulated lncRNAs in the initiation and evolution of cancer. However, there are still many knowledge gaps in the study of lncRNAs related to the prognosis and treatment of ESCA. In the literature search of lncRNA, we discovered TSPEAR-AS2, and found that the current reports on TSPEAR-AS2 in human cancer are very limited. To date, the role of TSPEAR-AS2 has been investigated in one study on gastric cancer and another on oral SCC, whereas its expression profile and prognostic significance in pan-cancer remain unclear. In this study, we conducted a comprehensive analysis to characterize the expression profile of TSPEAR-AS2 in human tumors and evaluate its relationship with prognosis. The results showed that TSPEAR-AS2 was dysregulated in various cancers, including ESCA, and its high expression was significantly associated with poor survival in patients with ESCA. ROC analysis showed that the AUC value of TSPEAR-AS2 was greater than 0.7 in multiple independent ESCA cohorts. These results suggest the clinical potential of TSPEAR-AS2 in the early diagnosis and prognostic evaluation of ESCA. However, multi-center, large-sample clinical studies are warranted to assess the reliability of TSPEAR-AS2 as a diagnostic and prognostic biomarker in ESCA.
Over-expression of oncogenic drivers is a crucial molecular event in tumorigenesis and can be regulated by both genetic and epigenetic mechanisms
30
–
32
. Post-transcriptional modification at the RNA level is a key reason for uncontrolled lncRNA expression and can drive tumor progression
33
,
34
. To explore the epigenetic mechanism underlying the up-regulation of TSPEAR-AS2 in ESCA, we analyzed the relationship between a panel of RNA modifiers and TSPEAR-AS2 expression. The results showed that METTL1 was positively correlated with TSPEAR-AS2 expression and up-regulated in ESCA tumor samples. Over-expression of METTL1 led to a significant increase in TSPEAR-AS2 expression in ESCA cells. As an m7G transferase, METTL1 has recently been reported to be involved in the biological processes of various tumors
35
. Although this study preliminarily shows that METTL1 induces TSPEAR-AS2 expression in ESCA, its precise regulatory mechanism warrants further investigation.
Tumor progression is a complex process
36
,
37
. The clinical application of immune checkpoint inhibitors has helped improve the tumor treatment strategy; however, it is associated with certain potential risks
38
,
39
. Therefore, developing novel, more effective anti-cancer therapies is necessary. Targeting lncRNAs using nucleic acid-based drugs, including antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs), is a promising therapeutic strategy with high clinical value and good application prospects for many diseases, including cancer
40
,
41
. To understand the biological role of TSPEAR-AS2 in ESCA, we performed various in vitro and in vivo experiments. Knockdown of TSPEAR-AS2 significantly inhibited cell proliferation, metastasis, stemness, and tumor growth, whereas its over-expression promoted ESCA progression. In addition, intratuminal injection of an ASO targeting TSPEAR-AS2 effectively inhibited the growth of ESCA tumors in vivo. These results suggest that TSPEAR-AS2 is an oncogene that facilitates ESCA development. However, TSPEAR-AS2 as a therapeutic target for ESCA warrants continuous and in-depth evaluation. Cancer stem cells are considered one of the key causes of malignant tumor progression, recurrence, and treatment resistance. This study showed that TSPEAR-AS2 down-regulation significantly attenuated the stemness of ESCA cells. These results suggest that TSPEAR-AS2 may contribute to therapeutic resistance of ESCA, which should be validated through systematic studies.
Interferons are involved in many physiological and pathological processes, such as immunity, cell proliferation, and differentiation. Abnormal interferon signaling pathways are related to tumors and other diseases
42
,
43
. Therefore, research on interferon signaling pathways has attracted wide attention in the field of oncology. In ESCA, interferon signaling not only participates in the response to neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy, but also serves as a potential prognostic indicator and therapeutic target
44
,
45
. However, the upstream mechanism that regulates interferon signaling is yet to be fully understood. In this study, we employed quantitative proteomics to analyze protein changes in ESCA cells following TSPEAR-AS2 deletion. The results revealed that TSPEAR-AS2 could regulate the expression of multiple interferon signaling molecules, such as HLA-E, IRF3, and IFIT1. However, the precise mechanism through which TSPEAR-AS2 initiates interferon signaling warrants further investigation. In addition, improving the effects of immunotherapy is an important challenge at present. Given that TSPEAR-AS2 regulates interferon signaling, investigating whether TSPEAR-AS2 affects the response to immunotherapy in ESCA through interferon signaling is necessary.
In conclusion, this study uncovered that TSPEAR-AS2 is dysregulated in pan-cancer and that its high expression is a potential diagnostic and prognostic indicator for ESCA. TSPEAR-AS2 functions as a driver to promote ESCA metastasis, stemness maintenance, and tumor growth. Hence, TSPEAR-AS2 is a promising therapeutic target for ESCA. In addition, METTL1-mediated TSPEAR-AS2 aggravates the malignant phenotype of ESCA, possibly through interferon signaling. Despite these important findings, this study has some limitations and knowledge gaps that should be acknowledged. First, how can TSPEAR-AS2 be validated as a noninvasive diagnostic and prognostic marker for ESCA? To address this scientific issue, multi-center studies should be performed to collect serum samples and related clinical parameters from both ESCA patients and healthy participants to evaluate the reliability of TSPEAR-AS2 as a biomarker. Second, how to determine whether TSPEAR-AS2 can be used as a therapeutic target for ESCA? To achieve this objective, novel oligonucleotide delivery systems should be used to target TSPEAR-AS2 for the treatment of ESCA in animal models in vivo. In the next few years, the development of effective early diagnostic biomarkers, prognostic indicators, and targeted therapies is expected to improve the diagnosis and treatment of ESCA and other cancers.
